outline.section: H2: Why Coconut Oil Is Not Ideal for a Fresh Tattoo
outline.guidance: Explain the core problem: a fresh tattoo is essentially an open wound. Coconut oil is a heavy, occlusive oil with a comedogenic rating of 4 out of 5, meaning it can block pores and suffocate the skin. On healing tattooed skin, this can trap bacteria, increase the risk of infection, prevent the skin from breathing, and lead to excessive scabbing that pulls ink out. Cite a dermatological or wound-care source for the comedogenic rating and occlusive properties. Note that the thick consistency makes it hard to apply a thin layer, so people tend to over-apply. Mention that heavily scented or unrefined coconut oil adds additional irritation risk on broken skin. Keep the tone informative and non-alarmist — this is not about fear-mongering, just setting realistic expectations.

outline.section: H2: When It Is Safe to Use Coconut Oil on a Tattoo
outline.guidance: Clarify the timeline: most tattoos take 2–4 weeks to heal on the surface and up to 3–6 months for the deeper dermal layers to fully recover. Once peeling has stopped, there is no more scabbing, skin is no longer shiny or sore, and the area is not itchy from active healing — that is generally when coconut oil becomes a safe and beneficial option. At this stage, coconut oil's antimicrobial lauric acid content, deep moisturizing fatty acids, and anti-inflammatory properties can help keep the ink looking vibrant and the surrounding skin soft and healthy. Link internally to the coconut oil as moisturizer post and the organic coconut oil for skin post. Cite a credible source for lauric acid's antimicrobial properties.
